title: Preterm labour and birth
blurb: Apply NICE NG25 and Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 5: prevention with progesterone or cerclage, P-PROM, diagnosis by cervical length, tocolysis, steroids, magnesium for neuroprotection and the right place of birth.
question: Joy, 27+2 weeks pregnant with intact membranes, arrives on the labour ward with regular painful contractions. Which treatments should the midwife expect to be offered to improve her baby's outcome?

teach.h: Preterm labour: what and why it matters
teach.body: Preterm birth is birth before 37+0 weeks. NICE NG25 separates suspected preterm labour (symptoms, not yet confirmed) from diagnosed preterm labour (confirmed by assessment or a test) and established preterm labour (progressive dilatation from 4 cm with regular contractions). In plain English: the earlier the baby, the more each intervention matters. The midwife's role is to recognise it, start the right care in time, and make sure the baby is born in the right place.

children.edge: Previous spontaneous PTB (to 34+0) or loss (from 16+0) AND cervix 25 mm or less
children.label: Offer choice: progesterone or cerclage

children.edge: Short cervix plus previous P-PROM or cervical trauma
children.label: Consider cerclage

teach.caption: Progesterone starts between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks and continues until at least 34 weeks. Document a plan for removing any cerclage suture.

teach.h: P-PROM: preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
teach.body: Offer a speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid; if pooling is seen, no further test is needed. If not, test vaginal fluid with an IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 test; do not use nitrazine. With P-PROM, offer oral erythromycin 250 mg four times a day for up to 10 days or until established labour, whichever is sooner; do not give co-amoxiclav. Diagnose intrauterine infection from clinical assessment plus CRP, white cell count and CTG together, not any one alone.

steps.label: Clinical assessment
steps.sub: History, observations, speculum (then VE if needed)

steps.label: More than 15 mm
steps.sub: Preterm labour unlikely; think of other causes

teach.caption: SBL v3.2 (5.9) records that fetal fibronectin test cassettes have been discontinued, so cervical length is the test to know.

Offer
Consider or discuss
teach.caption: If nifedipine is contraindicated, offer an oxytocin receptor antagonist. Do not offer betamimetics. No more than 2 courses of corticosteroids.

teach.caption: Given in established preterm labour or when birth is planned within 24 hours.

teach.caption: At birth: wait at least 60 seconds before clamping the cord, with the baby at or below the level of the placenta (NG25 1.14).

items: Joy has regular contractions and intact membranes. At under 30 weeks, she is treated as being in preterm labour after clinical assessment.
She is offered nifedipine tocolysis (26+0 to 33+6) and a course of corticosteroids (24+0 to 33+6).
At 27+2 weeks the SBL under-27-weeks NICU rule does not apply; the midwife informs the neonatal team and checks the local unit can provide the care her baby needs.
Labour establishes after transfer: magnesium sulfate 4 g over 15 minutes then 1 g per hour, with 4-hourly checks.
At birth, the cord is clamped after at least 60 seconds with the baby kept warm and at or below placental level.

teach.text: Erythromycin, not co-amoxiclav, for P-PROM (co-amoxiclav is specifically not offered). And nifedipine, not betamimetics, for tocolysis. Cervical length cut-offs differ by purpose: 25 mm or less at 16-24 weeks for PREVENTION; 15 mm or less from 30 weeks to DIAGNOSE preterm labour.

items: Prevention: history plus cervix 25 mm or less at 16-24 weeks: choice of progesterone or cerclage.
P-PROM: speculum for pooling; erythromycin 250 mg QDS up to 10 days; no co-amoxiclav.
29+6 or less: treat on clinical assessment. 30+0+: cervical length; 15 mm or less = preterm labour.
Offer nifedipine 26+0-33+6, steroids 24+0-33+6, magnesium 24+0-29+6 (4 g then 1 g/h).
Under 27 weeks, under 800 g, or multiples under 28 weeks: born on a NICU site. Delay cord clamping at least 60 s.

summary: You can now explain how preterm birth is prevented, how P-PROM and preterm labour are diagnosed, and which treatments NG25 offers at each gestation. You can also give magnesium sulfate safely and use SBL v3 element 5 to plan the right place of birth.

A.q: A woman at 31 weeks has P-PROM confirmed by pooling on speculum examination. Which antibiotic does NICE NG25 recommend?
options: Oral erythromycin 250 mg four times a day
Co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times a day
Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice a day
A.why: NG25 1.4.1: offer oral erythromycin 250 mg four times a day for a maximum of 10 days or until established labour, whichever is sooner.

whyNot.1: NG25 1.4.3: do not offer co-amoxiclav as prophylaxis for intrauterine infection in P-PROM.
whyNot.2: Intrapartum antibiotics follow NG195; P-PROM prophylaxis is oral erythromycin.
whyNot.3: Metronidazole is not the NG25 prophylaxis for P-PROM.

A.q: At 32 weeks, a woman with suspected preterm labour has a transvaginal cervical length of 22 mm. How should this be interpreted?
A.why: NG25 1.7.4: a cervical length of more than 15 mm means preterm labour is unlikely; think about alternative diagnoses and discuss going home versus monitoring.

whyNot.1: Preterm labour is diagnosed if cervical length is 15 mm or less.
whyNot.2: Cervical length and fibronectin are not used together, and fibronectin cassettes have been discontinued.
whyNot.3: Cerclage is a preventive option at 16-24 weeks, not a response to symptoms at 32 weeks.

A.q: A woman at 28+4 weeks with intact membranes is in suspected preterm labour. Which tocolytic should be offered?
A.why: NG25 1.8.3: offer nifedipine for tocolysis between 26+0 and 33+6 weeks with intact membranes in suspected or diagnosed preterm labour.

whyNot.0: Salbutamol is a betamimetic; NG25 1.8.5 says do not offer betamimetics for tocolysis.
whyNot.1: Terbutaline is also a betamimetic and should not be offered for tocolysis.
whyNot.2: An oxytocin receptor antagonist is offered if nifedipine is contraindicated, not as first choice.

B.q: A woman at 26+5 weeks is in established preterm labour. Which magnesium sulfate regimen does NICE recommend for fetal neuroprotection?
options: 4 g IV over 15 min, then 1 g/hour
2 g IV over 5 min, then 2 g/hour
4 g IM, then 4 g IM every 4 hours
1 g IV over 15 min, then 0.5 g/hour
B.why: NG25 1.10.4: 4 g IV bolus over 15 minutes, then 1 g per hour until the birth or for 24 hours, whichever is sooner.

whyNot.1: Neither the bolus nor the infusion rate matches NG25.
whyNot.2: NICE uses the intravenous regimen, not intramuscular doses.
whyNot.3: Both doses are below the NG25 regimen.

B.q: Between which gestations does NICE NG25 say corticosteroids should be OFFERED to women in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour?
B.why: NG25 1.9.2: offer maternal corticosteroids between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks.

whyNot.0: At 22+0 to 23+6, steroids are discussed with the woman and MDT rather than routinely offered.
whyNot.1: At 34+0 to 35+6, steroids are considered rather than offered.
whyNot.3: This range does not match the NICE window.

B.q: A woman on magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection develops oliguria. What does NG25 advise?
options: Monitor more often; reduce or stop
Give a fluid bolus of 1 litre
B.why: NG25 1.10.6: with oliguria or other evidence of renal failure, monitor more frequently for magnesium toxicity and reduce or stop the dose.

whyNot.0: Increasing the rate raises the risk of toxicity when excretion is poor.
whyNot.2: A large fluid bolus is not the NG25 response and risks fluid overload.
whyNot.3: Oliguria increases toxicity risk, so the infusion cannot simply continue unchanged.

C.q: Maya has had a previous spontaneous preterm birth at 31 weeks. A transvaginal scan at 19 weeks shows a cervical length of 22 mm. What should she be offered?
options: A choice of progesterone or cerclage
C.why: NG25 1.2.1: history of spontaneous preterm birth up to 34+0 plus cervical length 25 mm or less at 16+0-24+0: offer a choice of vaginal progesterone or cerclage.

whyNot.0: Monitoring alone withholds a recommended preventive treatment.
whyNot.1: Bed rest is not an NG25 preventive treatment.
whyNot.3: Nifedipine is a tocolytic for suspected preterm labour, not prophylaxis.

C.q: At 25+4 weeks, a singleton is in threatened preterm labour in a local neonatal unit hospital without a NICU. What does SBL v3.2 element 5 advise?
options: Birth locally with a NICU retrieval team
Transfer after the birth if needed
In utero transfer to a NICU site
C.why: SBL v3.2 5.18: babies under 27 weeks (and under 800 g, or multiples under 28 weeks) should be born in a maternity service on the same site as a NICU.

whyNot.0: Postnatal retrieval is less safe than being born on a NICU site, which SBL aims for.
whyNot.1: Steroids are important, but she should also give birth on a NICU site.
whyNot.2: Ex utero transfer is what the element aims to avoid for babies under 27 weeks.

C.q: A woman with suspected P-PROM at 30 weeks has no pooling on speculum examination. What should happen next?
options: IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 test of fluid
C.why: NG25 1.3.1: if pooling is not observed, perform an insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 or placental alpha-microglobulin-1 test of vaginal fluid.

whyNot.0: NG25 1.3.4: do not use nitrazine to diagnose P-PROM.
whyNot.2: Antibiotics are offered once P-PROM is confirmed or care is given as if it is; a negative test means no antibiotics.
whyNot.3: Digital examination is not the next diagnostic step for suspected P-PROM.

reteach.title: Prevent, diagnose, protect, place
reteach.question: Can you sort every preterm intervention into one of four jobs: prevent it, diagnose it, protect the baby, or get the baby born in the right place?

blocks.body: Prevent: progesterone or cerclage for a short cervix at 16-24 weeks with a history. Diagnose: clinical assessment, then cervical length from 30 weeks (15 mm or less means preterm labour). Protect the baby: steroids for the lungs, magnesium for the brain, nifedipine to buy time for both. Place: under 27 weeks, under 800 g or multiples under 28 weeks are born on a NICU site; at birth, wait at least 60 seconds before clamping the cord.

blocks.h: Upper gestation where each is OFFERED

blocks.text: Magnesium is OFFERED only to 29+6; from 30+0 to 33+6 it is CONSIDERED. Steroids are OFFERED to 33+6 and CONSIDERED 34+0 to 35+6.

explain.body: History of spontaneous preterm birth (to 34+0) or loss (from 16+0) plus cervix 25 mm or less at 16+0-24+0: offer progesterone or cerclage. Either alone: consider progesterone. Short cervix plus previous P-PROM or cervical trauma: consider cerclage (NG25 1.2).

test.q: A woman is started on vaginal progesterone because of a short cervix. Until when should it continue?
test.why: NG25 1.2.3: start between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks and continue until at least 34 weeks.

whyNot.0: 24 weeks is the latest start point, not the stopping point.
whyNot.1: Stopping at 28 weeks is earlier than NICE advises.
whyNot.3: NICE says at least 34 weeks, not a fixed 37 weeks.

explain.body: Speculum for pooling; if none, IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 test; no nitrazine. Erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for up to 10 days or until established labour; oral penicillin if erythromycin unsuitable; no co-amoxiclav. Infection is judged from clinical assessment plus CRP, white cell count and CTG together.

test.q: A woman with P-PROM at 30 weeks is well and apyrexial with a normal CTG, but one CRP result is raised. How should the team use this result?
options: Together with her clinical picture and tests
As a trigger for immediate birth
test.why: NG25 1.5.1-1.5.3: diagnose intrauterine infection using clinical assessment plus CRP, white cell count and CTG together; if they disagree, keep observing and consider repeating the tests.

whyNot.0: A single CRP must not be used in isolation to confirm infection.
whyNot.2: A raised CRP is not dismissed as expected; it is weighed with the clinical picture and other tests.
whyNot.3: One isolated raised CRP with a well woman and normal CTG does not by itself indicate birth.

explain.body: 29+6 or less: treat on clinical assessment. 30+0 or more: consider transvaginal cervical length; more than 15 mm, preterm labour unlikely; 15 mm or less, diagnosed preterm labour. If no test is done, treat as preterm labour (NG25 1.7).

test.q: A woman at 28 weeks has regular painful contractions and the clinical assessment suggests preterm labour. What should happen?
options: Discharge if the CTG is normal
test.why: NG25 1.7.3: at 29+6 weeks or less, if clinical assessment suggests preterm labour, advise treatment for preterm labour.

whyNot.0: Cervical length is used as a diagnostic test from 30+0 weeks.
whyNot.1: A normal CTG does not exclude preterm labour.
whyNot.2: Fibronectin is not used before 30 weeks, and its cassettes have been discontinued (SBL v3.2).

explain.body: Nifedipine (offer 26+0-33+6), steroids (offer 24+0-33+6; maximum 2 courses), magnesium (offer 24+0-29+6; 4 g over 15 min then 1 g/h). Born on a NICU site if under 27 weeks, under 800 g, or multiples under 28 weeks. Delay cord clamping at least 60 seconds.

test.q: What is the maximum number of courses of maternal corticosteroids NICE recommends for preterm birth?
test.why: NG25 1.9.5: do not give more than 2 courses of maternal corticosteroids for preterm birth.

whyNot.0: A single repeat course can be considered in some women, so the maximum is 2.
whyNot.3: 4 courses far exceeds the NICE maximum.
